pKa is defined as −log Ka, so the relationship runs the opposite way to acid strength:
the **stronger** the acid, the larger its Ka, and therefore the **smaller** its pKa.
Comparing the four values:
1.0 < 2.0 < 3.0 < 4.5
The smallest is 1.0, so that belongs to the strongest acid ✓
To see the size of the difference: pKa 1.0 means Ka = 10⁻¹ = 0.1, while pKa 4.5 means
Ka = 10⁻⁴·⁵ ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵. The first acid is some three thousand times the stronger.
The logarithm compresses a huge range into small numbers, which is why a difference of one
pKa unit is a tenfold difference in strength.
The instinct to pick the largest number is what the question is testing.
∴ 1.0.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|48||0|0.s:
An unsaturated fatty acid contains at least one C=C double bond; a saturated one has none.
(2) Palmitic acid, C₁₅H₃₁COOH — fully saturated
(3) Stearic acid, C₁₇H₃₅COOH — fully saturated
(4) Lauric acid, C₁₁H₂₃COOH — fully saturated
(1) **Oleic acid**, C₁₇H₃₃COOH — has one cis double bond at C-9 ✓
The formulae themselves give it away: a saturated acid fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH, and oleic acid is
two hydrogens short of that, which is the signature of one double bond.
That single cis bond puts a kink in the chain so the molecules cannot pack closely, which is
why oleic acid is a **liquid** at room temperature while stearic acid, with the same 18
carbons, is a waxy solid. It is the main constituent of olive oil.
∴ oleic acid.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|49||0|0:
Nylon-6,6 is made by condensing hexamethylenediamine with adipic acid, losing water at each
link:
n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH ⇒ [–NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
Now check each description.
(1) Copolymer ✓ — it is built from **two different** monomers.
(3) Condensation polymer ✓ — a small molecule, water, is eliminated at every step.
(4) Polyamide ✓ — the repeating link is the amide group –CO–NH–.
(2) **Homopolymer** ✗ — a homopolymer is made from a single repeating monomer, as
polythene is from ethene. Nylon-6,6 needs two, so it cannot be one.
The '6,6' itself records this: six carbons in the diamine and six in the diacid.
(Nylon-6, made from a single monomer caprolactam, *is* a homopolymer — which is exactly the
distinction being probed.)
∴ nylon is not a homopolymer.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|50||0|0:
Coal tar is separated by fractional distillation, and each fraction is collected over a
temperature range:
Light oil, up to 170 °C — benzene, toluene, xylene
**Middle oil**, 170–230 °C — **phenol**, naphthalene, cresols ✓
Heavy oil, 230–270 °C — naphthalene, cresols, quinoline
Green oil (anthracene oil), 270–360 °C — anthracene, phenanthrene
Residue — pitch
Phenol is recovered from the middle oil by shaking with sodium hydroxide: being acidic, it
dissolves as sodium phenoxide while the neutral naphthalene does not, and acidifying the
extract liberates the phenol again.
The middle fraction is also called carbolic oil for precisely this reason — carbolic acid being
the old name for phenol.
∴ middle oil.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|52||0|0:
Froth flotation works on wettability. The pulped ore is treated with a collector such as
potassium ethyl xanthate or pine oil, which coats the **sulphide mineral** particles and leaves
a hydrocarbon layer facing outwards.
That layer is non-polar, so the ore surface is **not wetted by water** ✓ Instead it attaches
itself to the air bubbles blown through the pulp and is carried up into the froth, which is
skimmed off.
The gangue — silicates and oxides — has a polar surface that water wets readily, so it stays
in the water and sinks.
So the separation rests entirely on a difference in surface wettability, deliberately created
by the collector.
(1) is wrong — both ore and gangue are insoluble. (4) is wrong — the ore particles are
generally **denser** than the gangue, which is why gravity separation would fail and flotation
is needed. (2) plays no part.
∴ because their surface is not easily wetted by water.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|53||0|0:
Find the false statement about amorphous solids.
(1) True — there is no long-range orderly arrangement; the particles are arranged randomly,
like a frozen liquid.
(2) True — they are rigid and incompressible, which is why they count as solids at all.
(3) True — having no single regular lattice, they have no sharp melting point and soften over
a **range** of temperature. Glass is the standard example.
(4) **False** — amorphous solids are **isotropic**, not anisotropic. Because the arrangement is
random, it looks statistically the same in every direction, so properties such as refractive
index, conductivity and mechanical strength are identical whichever way you measure them.
It is **crystalline** solids that are anisotropic: their regular lattice differs along different
directions, so their properties do too.
Amorphous solids are also described as pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids for the same
underlying reason.
∴ statement (4) is incorrect.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|54||0|0.s:
Graham's law of diffusion states that the rate is inversely proportional to the square root of
the molar mass:
rate ∝ 1/√M
So for two gases:
r(H₂)/r(A) = √(M_A/M_H₂)
Hydrogen diffuses six times faster, so the left-hand side is 6:
6 = √(M_A/2)
Square both sides:
36 = M_A/2
M_A = 72 g mol⁻¹
Note the square root is what makes the mass ratio so much larger than the rate ratio — a
sixfold difference in speed means a thirty-sixfold difference in mass.
The common error is to answer 12, by forgetting to square, which is where the smaller
options come from.
∴ 72.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|56||0|0.s:
Physical adsorption is held by van der Waals forces, so a gas is adsorbed more strongly the
more its own molecules attract one another. That tendency is measured by how easily the gas
liquefies — its **critical temperature**.
Compare the critical temperatures:
H₂ 33 K, N₂ 126 K, O₂ 154 K, **SO₂ 430 K**
Sulphur dioxide has by far the highest, so it is the most easily liquefiable and the most
readily adsorbed ✓
Hydrogen, at the other extreme, is the hardest gas of the four to liquefy and is adsorbed
least.
The amounts are strikingly different in practice: one gram of activated charcoal adsorbs
roughly 380 cm³ of SO₂ against about 4 cm³ of hydrogen.
SO₂ is also polar, which helps further, but the critical temperature is the general rule.
∴ SO₂.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|57||0|0:
Sodium chloride has the rock-salt structure, in which Na⁺ and Cl⁻ alternate along every edge
of the cube, each ion octahedrally surrounded by six of the other kind.
The distance between a neighbouring Na⁺ and Cl⁻ is therefore **half** the edge length.
Walking along one edge you pass:
half a Cl⁻ ... a whole Na⁺ ... half a Cl⁻
which is two Na⁺–Cl⁻ separations end to end.
So if that separation is X pm:
a = 2X pm
The relation is often written a = 2(r₊ + r₋), and X is exactly the sum (r₊ + r₋) — the
centre-to-centre distance of touching ions.
Option (1), X/2, inverts the relationship, and option (3), 4X, would be the body diagonal
rather than the edge.
∴ 2X pm.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|58||0|0:
In Werner's terms the **primary** valency is the oxidation state, satisfied by negative ions,
and the **secondary** valency is the coordination number, satisfied by ligands. A **negatively
charged ligand** can satisfy both at once.
(2) [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ — NH₃ is **neutral**, so it can only satisfy the secondary valency (4). The
primary valency (+2) is satisfied by the sulphate outside ✓ correct as stated.
(1) K₄[Fe(CN)₆] — Fe²⁺ with six CN⁻. The cyanides satisfy all six secondary valencies, and two
of them also satisfy the primary valency of +2 ✓ correct.
(4) K₃[Fe(CN)₆] — Fe³⁺ with six CN⁻. Six secondary valencies, and three of the cyanides also
satisfy the primary valency of +3 ✓ correct.
(3) **Incorrect** — this says the ligand satisfies *only* the secondary valency in K₃[Fe(CN)₆],
which contradicts (4). Since CN⁻ is anionic, it necessarily does both.
∴ statement (3) is incorrect.
kcet|Chemistry|2004|59||0|0:
Acetoxybenzoic acid is **aspirin**, acetylsalicylic acid — salicylic acid with its phenolic –OH
acetylated.
Its uses are:
**antipyretic** — it lowers a raised body temperature ✓
analgesic — it relieves pain
anti-inflammatory, and in low doses an antiplatelet agent used to prevent heart attacks
The acetylation matters: salicylic acid itself is too irritating to the stomach lining to be
taken by mouth, and converting the phenolic OH to an ester makes it tolerable.
Of the options, only antipyretic describes aspirin.
(1) An antiseptic kills microorganisms on living tissue — that is Dettol or iodine.
(3) An antimalarial is chloroquine or quinine.
(4) An antidepressant is a drug such as imipramine.
Aspirin works by inhibiting the enzyme that makes prostaglandins, which mediate both fever
and pain.
∴ an antipyretic.

kcet|Chemistry|2004|60||0|0.s:
The distinction is whether a phosphate group is present.
**Nucleoside** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar
**Nucleotide** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate
A nucleoside has no phosphate, so hydrolysing it can only give back its two components:
nucleoside + H₂O ⇒ heterocyclic base + pentose sugar
The sugar is ribose or deoxyribose, both **aldopentoses** — five carbons with an aldehyde
group. The base is adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine or uracil, all **heterocyclic**, having
nitrogen atoms in the ring.
So the products are an aldopentose and a heterocyclic base ✓
Options (2) and (3) both include orthophosphoric acid, which would only appear on hydrolysing
a **nucleotide**. That is exactly the distinction the question is testing.
∴ an aldopentose and a heterocyclic base.
